title: Equality, types and hoisting
summary: Why === is safer than ==, what typeof tells you, and how JavaScript moves declarations to the top.

sections.heading: == converts, === does not
body: `==` converts both sides to the same type before comparing, which gives surprising results. `===` only says true when both the type and the value match. Use `===`.
TypeScript reports most of these mixed comparisons as errors before the code runs, so this example is plain JavaScript.

javascript.code:
console.log(1 == '1')
console.log(1 === '1')
console.log(0 == '')
console.log(null == undefined)
console.log(null === undefined)

sections.heading: typeof tells you the kind of value
body: `typeof` gives a string naming the type. Two traps: arrays say `"object"` (use `Array.isArray`), and so does `null`.

javascript.code:
console.log(typeof 42, typeof 'hi', typeof true)
console.log(typeof [], typeof null, typeof undefined)
console.log(Array.isArray([]))
javascript.output:
number string boolean
object object undefined
true

sections.heading: Hoisting
body: Before running, JavaScript reads all declarations. Function declarations can be called before the line where they are written.
A `var` exists from the start too, but its value is `undefined` until its line runs. `let` and `const` are stricter: using them before their line throws a `ReferenceError`.

mistakes: Using `==` and getting a "true" you did not expect.
Checking `typeof x === 'array'`. That is never true; use `Array.isArray(x)`.
Using `var`. Prefer `const`, and `let` when the value has to change.
